passage:
Monday: Arnab, sixteen, forwarded a message to his class group: "Drinking cold water after meals causes serious illness." Yamini replied, "Source?" Arnab typed, "Everyone knows this," and felt annoyed that she was questioning him in front of everyone.
Wednesday: Still irritated, he searched to prove her wrong. Every reliable site he found said the claim had no evidence. He noticed he had been hunting only for pages that agreed with him.
The next Monday: He posted, "I was wrong about the cold water thing. I believed it because my Nani says it, and I didn't check." Yamini sent a thumbs up. Arnab felt strangely lighter.

qa.q: What did Yamini reply to Arnab's message?
qa.a: She replied, "Source?"

qa.q: Why did Arnab feel annoyed on Monday?
qa.a: He felt challenged in front of everyone, and his confidence in the message made the question feel like an attack.

qa.q: What was the key moment of change for Arnab?
qa.a: Noticing he had been searching only for pages that agreed with him, which let him see his own bias.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Arnab's public correction?
qa.a: She probably respects him more for admitting he was wrong, which is why she sent a thumbs up.

grounding: It shows a teenager noticing his own confirmation bias and publicly admitting the limits of what he knew.

passage: Arnab, when I was fifteen, I was sure my best friend Neelam hated me. She didn't wave one morning, and by lunch I had decided she was jealous of my marks. I felt it so strongly that it had to be true. I stopped talking to her for two weeks. Then her brother said, "Jyoti, our grandmother was in hospital that week." She hadn't even seen me that morning. I remember sitting on the school steps, hot-faced, realising that a strong feeling had made me certain, not any fact. Since then, when I'm very sure about what someone thinks, I ask myself: what do I actually know? Usually it's much less than I feel.

qa.q: How long did young Jyoti stop talking to Neelam?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What did Jyoti realise, hot-faced, on the school steps?
qa.a: That a strong feeling, not any fact, had made Jyoti certain about Neelam's motives, and it brought shame.

qa.q: What question does Jyoti now ask herself, and why does it help?
qa.a: "What do I actually know?" It separates facts from feelings before deciding what someone thinks.

qa.q: How might Neelam have experienced those two weeks?
qa.a: Already worried about her grandmother, she probably felt confused and hurt that her friend suddenly went cold.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager recognising that emotional reasoning had created certainty without facts.

passage: The physics project was due at nine the next morning, and the lab readings made no sense. Bidisha, seventeen, was sure her method was right; she'd topped the last test. When Suraj said, "Maybe we measured the length wrong," she snapped, "I did that part. It's fine." It was eleven at night and the power kept flickering. Suraj quietly re-measured by torchlight. Four centimetres off. Bidisha stared at the ruler. Her face burned. She thought of how quickly she'd dismissed him, just because she'd done well before. "You're right. I was sure because I'm usually right, which isn't a reason." They redid the graph by one in the morning. It came out straight.

qa.q: How far off was the measurement?
qa.a: Four centimetres.

qa.q: What did Bidisha realise about herself when she stared at the ruler?
qa.a: That her certainty came from past success rather than checking, and she felt embarrassed for dismissing Suraj.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do in future group work?
qa.a: Treat a teammate's doubt as a reason to check rather than a challenge, especially under time pressure.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when she snapped at him?
qa.a: Brushed off, yet he chose to re-measure quietly rather than argue, which kept the project on track.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising overconfidence as a bias and admitting the limits of her knowledge under deadline pressure.

passage: Varun had been sure since Monday: the new chemistry teacher disliked him. She had cut four marks on his practical file, and he told everyone at the Salt Lake bus stop. On Thursday, Deepika showed him her file. Four marks cut too, for the same missing diagrams. 'She wrote the same comment on mine,' Deepika said. Varun felt his face heat up. He opened his file again and actually read the red ink. It was specific, even polite. 'I think I decided she hated me because I felt bad,' he said slowly, 'and then I only noticed things that fit.' Deepika grinned. 'So, apologise to the bus stop?' 'Maybe just redraw the diagrams first.'

qa.q: How many marks were cut from Varun's file?
qa.a: Four marks were cut.

qa.q: What made Varun's face heat up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed once Deepika's file showed the same cut and comment, proving his story about the teacher was wrong.

qa.q: What habit could help Varun next time he feels treated unfairly?
qa.a: He could read the actual feedback and compare with others before deciding someone is against him.

qa.q: What would change if Varun had kept telling his story at the bus stop?
qa.a: Other students might have started seeing the teacher as unfair without reason, hurting her start at the school.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising that his hurt feelings shaped his belief and that he only noticed evidence that fit it.

passage:
'Auto is always faster than the bus to Nani's. Always.'
'Payal, last week the auto took forty minutes,' said her brother Amandeep, not looking up from his laptop.
'That was one time. Traffic.'
'And the one time you took the bus?'
'...It came quickly. But that was luck.'
'So when the auto is slow, it's traffic, and when the bus is fast, it's luck?'
Payal opened her mouth, then closed it. 'Okay, that sounds bad when you say it.'
'I'm not saying the bus is faster. I don't know either.'
'Then why are you arguing?'
'I'm not. I'm asking how you know.'
She thought. 'I don't, really. I just hate the bus because it's crowded.'
'That's a real reason. Just not a speed reason.'
'Fine. Let's time both next month.'

qa.q: How long did the auto take last week?
qa.a: It took forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Payal realise when she said 'that sounds bad when you say it'?
qa.a: She realised she had been explaining away evidence that did not fit her belief, and felt a bit embarrassed at being caught out.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's approach get right?
qa.a: He asked how she knew instead of claiming the opposite, which let her find the flaw herself.

qa.q: What would change if Amandeep had just said 'you're wrong'?
qa.a: Payal would likely have dug in and defended the auto instead of admitting she didn't really know.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager noticing that dislike of the bus, not evidence, was driving her certainty, and admitting what she does not know.

passage: I'm Madhav. In Class 11 a new boy, Sumit, joined from Delhi. He spoke fast, used big words, and answered first in every class. I decided in two days that he was arrogant. Everything he did after that seemed to prove it. Then we were put together for a chemistry project. At my house, he admitted he talked fast because he was nervous in new places. I realised I'd only noticed things that fit my first idea. I'd made up my mind and then collected evidence. Now I try to wait a week before I judge anyone.

qa.q: Where did Sumit join from?
qa.a: From Delhi.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel on realising the judgement about Sumit was wrong?
qa.a: Madhav felt embarrassed and humbled, seeing that the first idea had shaped everything noticed after.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav for meeting new people?
qa.a: Keep waiting before judging, and look for evidence that could prove the first impression wrong.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt in those first days at the new school?
qa.a: Nervous and out of place, even while seeming confident.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising confirmation bias in a snap judgement about a new classmate.

passage:
Debate coach's note, Harish, January
Sabina (16) argued this week that exams should be scrapped. In the rebuttal, she said, "Everyone I know hates exams, so they're bad." Then she stopped mid-sentence and said, "Actually, that's just my feeling. I need evidence." The room went quiet. She asked for a minute, then argued from research on stress and learning instead. I told her afterwards that catching her own emotional reasoning mid-debate was the best moment of the session. I'm adding a short bias-spotting exercise to next week's practice, and I've asked Sabina to lead the first round.

qa.q: What did Sabina argue should be scrapped?
qa.a: Exams.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: She was probably unsettled and a bit embarrassed, realising her point rested on feeling, not evidence.

qa.q: Why is Harish's bias-spotting exercise a good next step?
qa.a: It helps the whole team practise catching emotional reasoning the way Sabina did.

qa.q: How might the other debaters see Sabina's moment?
qa.a: They might respect her honesty and feel encouraged to check their own reasoning.

grounding: Shows a teenager catching her own emotional reasoning mid-debate, noted by her coach.

passage:
Usha's diary, Thursday
Today I fought with Minakshi about a message going round the class group saying the board exams were cancelled. I was so sure it was true. I even argued with her in front of everyone. Then she asked, "Where did it come from?" I didn't know. I checked the board's website, and there was nothing. I believed it because I wanted it to be true. That's embarrassing to write. Minakshi was kind about it. Tomorrow I'll say sorry. Rule for me: if I really want something to be true, check it twice.

qa.q: What did the message claim?
qa.a: That the board exams were cancelled.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after checking the website?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed and humbled, seeing that wanting it to be true had clouded her judgement.

qa.q: What could Usha do before believing the next forwarded message?
qa.a: Check where it came from and look at the official source first.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Usha says sorry?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, glad their friendship survived the argument.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising that her wishes shaped her belief in a rumour.

passage: When Kalyani Ma'am took over science at the Bijapur school, Vikas decided on day one that she was strict and unfair. She didn't smile, she wore thick glasses and she made them sit in alphabetical order. He told everyone. For two weeks he barely listened. Then his test came back with a note: "Your reasoning in Q3 is excellent. Come and see me about the next level problems." Vikas stared at it. At break he watched her help a struggling girl patiently for ten minutes. He felt his face go hot. He had made up his mind based on her glasses and her face. "I got her completely wrong," he told his friend. "And I told everyone." He went to see her after school, still embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Kalyani Ma'am write about Q3?
qa.a: "Your reasoning in Q3 is excellent."

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when his face went hot?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and embarrassed, realising he had judged her on appearance.

qa.q: What could Vikas do about the things he told everyone?
qa.a: He could tell his friends honestly that he was wrong about her.

qa.q: How might Kalyani Ma'am see Vikas when he comes to see her?
qa.a: She may see a capable student who is finally engaging, without knowing what he had assumed.

grounding: A teen realises he judged a new teacher unfairly from first impressions and admits the bias.

passage: In the Osaka high school's debate club, Yuki argued hard that phones should be banned in classrooms. She'd felt so sure. But Olga, the exchange student from Riga, asked quietly, "Why do you think that?" "Because phones are distracting." "Do you have data?" Yuki paused. She didn't. She'd been angry at her little brother for being on his phone all weekend, and she'd carried that feeling into the argument. That night, she looked up studies. Some said phones distracted; others said they helped some students. She wrote in her notebook: "Feeling strongly isn't evidence." At the next session, she began, "I was too sure last time." Olga smiled.

qa.q: Where was Olga from?
qa.a: Riga.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel when Olga asked if she had data?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and a bit embarrassed, realising her certainty came from anger rather than evidence.

qa.q: What worked in how Yuki responded to her mistake?
qa.a: She looked up studies and admitted she had been too sure, instead of defending her view.

qa.q: How might Olga see Yuki's opening line at the next session?
qa.a: Olga would likely respect Yuki's honesty and feel glad the question helped.

grounding: A Japanese teen realises her debating position came from emotional reasoning, not evidence.

passage:
At the Friday debate club, Lavanya, sixteen, was sure Ishita's argument about school uniforms was wrong. She stood to reply and said, "That's just silly."

The teacher asked, "Why?"

Lavanya opened her mouth and found she had no reason. She didn't like Ishita. They'd fought last month. She had decided the argument was silly because Ishita made it.

She sat down, cheeks hot.

After the debate, she went to Ishita. "Your point about cost was actually good. I dismissed it because... well. I was being unfair."

Ishita blinked. "Okay. Thanks."

That evening Lavanya wrote in her notebook: "Check: am I disagreeing with the idea, or the person?"

qa.q: What did Lavanya write in her notebook?
qa.a: "Check: am I disagreeing with the idea, or the person?"

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she realised she had no reason?
qa.a: Lavanya felt embarrassed, her cheeks hot, realising she was biased against Ishita.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do after recognising her bias?
qa.a: She admitted to Ishita that the point was good and she had been unfair, and wrote a reminder to check herself.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Lavanya's apology?
qa.a: Ishita was surprised but likely appreciated the honesty.

grounding: At a debate club, a teenager recognises that personal dislike was biasing her judgement and admits it.

passage:
Dear Neelam Ma'am,

I'm writing because I owe you an apology, and I think I owe myself an explanation.

Last week in class, I argued very strongly that the new exam pattern was unfair. I was sure. I said everyone agreed. When you asked for evidence, I said, "It just is."

I went home and looked it up. I found that the new pattern actually helps students like me in some ways. I had only read posts from people who were angry, and I'd been angry too, so it felt true.

I think I mistook my feeling for a fact. And I only looked at the side I already agreed with.

I'm sorry I was rude. Next time I'll read both sides before I argue.

Sunaina, Class 11 B

qa.q: What did Sunaina say when asked for evidence?
qa.a: Sunaina said, "It just is."

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel writing the letter?
qa.a: Sunaina feels sorry and a bit embarrassed, but also honest and reflective about the mistake.

qa.q: What did Sunaina learn about the limits of personal thinking?
qa.a: That feeling angry made the view seem true, and reading only one side hid the full picture.

qa.q: How might Neelam Ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Neelam Ma'am would likely feel touched and impressed by the honesty and self-reflection.

grounding: A teenager writes to a teacher recognising emotional reasoning and one-sided reading in an earlier argument.

passage:
Thanks, Sahil. So, I'm Irfan, I'm seventeen, and you asked about the video.

Last year a clip went round of a politician from a party I don't like saying something terrible. I believed it instantly. I shared it with a caption, "Told you so."

My cousin replied, "Check the date." I was annoyed. Obviously it was real, it matched everything I already thought.

Then I checked. It was cut. The full speech said the opposite. The clip had been edited to change the meaning.

I felt so stupid. Not because I was fooled; everyone gets fooled. But because I believed it only because I wanted to.

Now, when something makes me go "Yes! I knew it!", that's exactly when I slow down and check.

qa.q: What did Irfan's cousin reply?
qa.a: The cousin replied, "Check the date."

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after finding out the clip was edited?
qa.a: Irfan felt foolish and embarrassed, realising the belief came from wanting it to be true.

qa.q: What did Irfan change after this experience?
qa.a: Irfan now slows down and checks exactly when something confirms an existing belief.

qa.q: How might Irfan's cousin feel about Irfan's change?
qa.a: The cousin would likely feel glad that the reminder helped.

grounding: A teenager tells a podcast host how confirmation bias led to sharing an edited clip, and how checking comes first now.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and I sit next to Ankita in Class 11. In today's debate on whether homework should be banned, Ankita was brilliant for five minutes, until Harish quoted a survey that went against her. Her jaw tightened. She said, "That can't be right; everyone I know hates homework." Then she stopped mid-sentence. She looked at her notes for a long moment and said, "Actually, that's just my friends. I don't know what most students think. I'd need to read that survey before I argue with it." A few people laughed, surprised. I can't say what went on in her head, but later I saw her in the library with a printout of that survey.

qa.q: What was the debate topic?
qa.a: Whether homework should be banned.

qa.q: What does Ankita's tightened jaw suggest when the survey was quoted?
qa.a: It suggests she felt defensive and irritated to hear evidence against her side.

qa.q: What did Ankita's change of course get right?
qa.a: She noticed she was judging from her own friends, admitted she didn't know, and chose to read the evidence before arguing.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Ankita's change mid-debate?
qa.a: Lakshmi is struck by it, unsure what Ankita was thinking, but notices the follow-through in the library.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager catching herself generalising from her own circle and admitting the limits of what she knows.
